This study develops a flexible dynamic modeling framework capable of capturing the complex temporal dependencies observed in network traffic patterns. The proposed model, which extends the negative binomial regression approach, incorporates both the network's topological information and a temporal component similar to that used in ARMA/GARCH models. Additionally, the framework allows for time-varying parameters and enables easy adaptation to changing network conditions and external factors. The effectiveness of the proposed model is validated through simulation studies and an analysis of real-world network data, demonstrating its capability to accurately predict future network traffic patterns.

The paper examines the limitations of using stellar light curves from the ERNE system for aerosol monitoring, particularly in wide-field imaging, due to faint signals and wide acceptance angles. To demonstrate the system's capabilities and potential improvements, the ERNE array was used to monitor the curve of the supernova SN 2020fn in the M81 galaxy. The observations revealed a deep UV bump in the supernova's evolution that matched a model with low wind speeds and minimal aerosol content, confirming the system's ability to characterize aerosol conditions even in external galaxies, despite more precise results being possible for local observations.

Achieving precise and efficient configurational molecular sampling is a key aspect of Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations. While previous research has primarily used simple linear forces to describe particles' dynamics in configurational bias Monte Carlo (CBMC) simulations, our proposed approach employs a more accurate integrated Hamiltonian to enhance sampling efficiency. In CBMC simulations for large molecules such as polymers, the sheer number of proposed modifications often results in a low acceptance rate due to the principle of detailed balance. To address this, we implemented a biasing potential based on configurational bias to promote successful modifications. Our findings from testing both linear and non-linear models on a harmonic oscillator and a Lennard-Jones system demonstrate that the approach is capable of achieving efficient molecular sampling with reduced fluctuations in total energy over time. The results also reveal the benefit of the biasing potential in improving integration efficiency and support the suitability of MD simulations for molecular CBMC sampling, opening up the possibility of using Molecular Dynamics-generated states as input for Monte Carlo simulations, and allowing both techniques to be combined in a united algorithm.

Human reference information has been commonly used to evaluate the performance of automatic image description systems. This study aims to enhance the assessment of systems generating image descriptions by comparing them to judged descriptions provided by humans, judging accuracy based on relevance. To obtain these judgments, we conducted a large-scale study with 2000 participants, asking them to read given descriptions and provide corresponding visual explanations suitable for blind individuals. The dataset resulting from this study consists of 160000 description-judge pairs across 8000 images, with participants selecting from multiple description options or contributing original content. To further analyze the data, we conducted a judgment sub-study with 100 participants to judge the similarity between descriptions and visual explanations. The authors propose a sub-set of 200 images for more in-depth research, judging similarity based on a 7-point scale. The dataset is made available for system evaluation, with the research finding that comparing automatic descriptions to human judgment provides relevant feedback for improvement, though adjusted accuracy measures are necessary when assessing similarity.

We provide a novel source of technical constraints on the complexity of a specific rational conformal field theory by drawing an unexpected connection between mathematical areas. Initially, we establish the relevance of specific diagonal modular invariant partition functions within the S1111 torus theory, then we show their equivalence to solution methods for the Euler-Arnold equation associated with the $n$-punctured sphere theory, allowing us to leverage these solutions to determine the intricacy of the $n$-punctured sphere theory.

In search of an explanation for the universe's baryon asymmetry, theoretical models predict the existence of additional baryonic matter undetected thus far. Unlike dark matter, no specific characteristics are proposed for these hidden baryons. This report compiles predictions from various theories, presenting a loss function suitable for future experiments and cosmological observations, including those from spectroscopic surveys of the early universe and searches for primordial black holes, primordial gas clouds, and acute angle measurements between CMB lensing and polarization.

This report examines the performance of wideband waveforming as an alternative multiple access method in multiple-user systems that utilize multiple appliances per user and multiple carriers across multiple users. In a system with multiple appliances and multiple users, wideband waveforming can improve power distribution to the appliances while also enhancing overall data rates. Additionally, in a system with multiple users utilizing multiple appliances, wideband waveforming can reduce interference between users and increase overall data rates. Although the system with multiple appliances and multiple users is similar to a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system, the research indicates that wideband waveforming provides distinct benefits over traditional MIMO technology. To evaluate the performance of wideband waveforming, the paper utilizes the MATLAB simulation tool in a system with multiple appliances and multiple users.

We present a theory framework intended to support the fitting of observables as functions of a target variable, such as parton distribution functions (PDFs). This format is optimized for the graphical representation of PDFs. The paper outlines the PDF fit process, which involves the selection of a parametric function, the gathering of experimental and theoretical data, and the application of the framework to fit the PDFs in terms of fit parameters corresponding to the target variable. The article also discusses the derivation of $x$-dependent PDFs from the fit parameters and the subsequent graphical presentation of the results.

This study examines the dynamics of a methane jet fire under the influence of acoustic forcing to better understand the formation of fire whirls. Unlike conventional jet fire research that focuses on passive turbulence, this study investigates the active response of the flame to acoustic forcing. Through large-eddy simulations, the paper models the non-linear behavior of the jet fire in an turbulent flow, while also developing an active flame method to introduce vertical flame oscillations in response to acoustic forcing. Linearized RANS simulations are also performed to analyze the effects of various linearized forces, such as buoyancy, gravity, and pressure gradients, on the jet fire's behavior. Results show that the jet fire's response to acoustic forcing is primarily driven by the pressure gradient, with the active flame method effectively inducing flame oscillations that amplify the effects of nonlinear forcing. The study reveals that the non-linear response of the jet fire to acoustic forcing is mainly caused by the modulation of the flame's heat release rate, and the ultimate growth rate of the instability is influenced by the intensity of the acoustic forcing and the tip angle of the flame. The research provides valuable insights into the role of acoustic forcing in jet fire dynamics and can inform the design of more safe and efficient combustion systems.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory based on the use of information processing techniques. This paper aims to provide a concise overview of nonlocal gravity theory, detailing its fundamental constitutive assumptions and a systematic derivation of the field equations. Nonlocal gravity theory is shown to be closely related to another classical model, de Donder–Infeld–Sudan, though it differs in the absence of a local curvature term. The article also discusses the potential equivalence of nonlocal gravity theory to modified gravitational models with local curvature terms, such as $R^2$-gravity, under the assumption of weak gravitational fields. Furthermore, the paper suggests possible improvements to the theory that may account for the effects of quantum vacuum and Brownian motion within the framework of classical gravity theory.

The operation of particle accelerators to produce highly energetic collisions of particles leads to the creation of a state within the vacuum that is highly excited in the immediate area of the interaction. This state is highly unstable and results in the emission of low-energy particles through a process known as collective behavior, which leaves the area in a less excited state that is conducive to the successful operation of experiments with high-energy particle accelerators. In searches for the discovery of new and heavy particles, the ability to observe interactions between highly energetic particles is compromised by the background of low-energy particles remaining after the emission process. To address this issue, effective methods to reduce the background levels are necessary, which in turn will improve the sensitivity of the experiment in the search for new and heavy particles that are outside the reach of the highly energetic collisions. Such an approach is beneficial not only in the search for new particles but also in enabling precise measurements of the properties of well-known particles through the observation of interactions between highly energetic and low-energy particles. To demonstrate these benefits, we report the results of an search for the discovery of exotic particles that are coupled weakly, which have resulted in no new discoveries and have led to the development of a model that is informed by the data and the successful operation of the accelerator. Through this model, there is an increased limit on the ability of the axion-like particle to resolve a mystery regarding the nature of dark energy.

The paper examines the possible link between the magnetic field strength of a neutron star and the recurrence frequency of it becoming a visible X-ray binary transient. A potential correlation is found with the recurrence time that may correspond to the size of the neutron star's magnetic field. Additionally, the probable status of 14 X-ray binaries observed in the Galactic Centre is analyzed, suggesting that most are likely systems in which the companion star is a brown dwarf or planet. The paper concludes that tidal forces that may have affected the formation of these systems in the Centre could provide clues as to how massive stars end up in the Galactic Centre.

Bipartite graphs are structured as graphs with two parts, where edges only connect nodes from different parts. These graphs are important in many areas such as computer science, operations research, and social network analysis. The concept of independence within these graphs is defined by the greatest number of nodes from each part that do not share any connections, which is represented by the formula i(G). This value is particularly significant in understanding the structure of these networks. The polynomial that describes the colorings of these graphs is known as the Tutte-Grothendieck invariant, denoted as P_G(x). This invariant can be restructured into a more complex expression involving two linear factors, where the coefficients are related to the independence numbers of a series of subgraphs. The main contribution of this research is the development of an algorithm that can compute the independence numbers of subgraphs in constant time, given the network size, in order to factorize the invariant expression in similar constant time, given the network size, using FPT algorithms.

The demand for deeper energy savings in server-class systems has led to significant improvements in hardware designs, creating opportunities for more innovative and efficient approaches.  Although these systems have been designed with advanced features, such as performance curves that are not linear and the ability to operate at different frequencies and cores, current research is not optimized to take full advantage of these capabilities.  In contrast, existing methods that allow for reduced frequencies in servers are limited in their improvements, typically achieving only modest reductions in frequency that are not satisfactory.  A new strategy has been proposed with an efficient algorithm that allows the system to be run at significantly lower frequencies, such as the maximum initial frequency of the Intel Xeon E5-2690 v4, while still providing satisfactory performance for various workloads and scales beyond what is feasible for current hardware designs.  The results show that the new approach is capable of achieving substantial savings in energy consumption, allowing the system to be run at as low as 13% of the initial frequency, and is also beneficial for reducing the temperature of the components and may allow traditional methods of performance tuning to be applied to previously infeasible workloads.

This paper investigates the concept of unknotting links in both classical and welded unknotting theory. Within the welded context, we define a new operation called (diagonal) move and explore its implications. By extending previous research that included the flip move, we prove that the (diagonal) move and the flip move are equivalent. Furthermore, we establish that both classical and welded knots are (diagonal) simple, indicating that any classical or welded knot can be resolved into a simple loop through a series of (diagonal) moves. In addition, we also prove that welded links are (diagonal) compound, indicating that any welded link can be separated into individual components through (diagonal) moves. The (diagonal) move's distinct properties in relation to classical, welded, and additional invariants make it a promising area of study. The (diagonal) move's impact on various invariants, including the Miloto invariant, the anti-casimir invariant, the WRT invariants, the Lyng invariant, and the Le invariant, are explored in the paper, providing evidence of the (diagonal) move's effect on these invariants. The (diagonal) move's relation to other unknotting operations, such as the unknotting value, the defect, and the minimum number of moves required to unknot, are also examined, laying the groundwork for future research on unknotting theory, particularly in the context of the (diagonal) move. This paper explores how a team of autonomous robots can work together to determine the outcome of a voting system in a democratic process. The voters in this system are the robots themselves, and they are limited in their ability to exchange information with one another due to their physical arrangement into disjoint clusters. To overcome these communication barriers, the robots engage in a random walk to exchange local information about the outcome. What makes this problem unique is its connection to a dynamic environment, as the robots' movement directly impacts their ability to share information. We develop a comprehensive model that accounts for the simultaneous occurrence of the environment's changes and the robots' random walk, and derive an equation to determine how quickly information about the outcome spreads throughout the team. In a numerical example, we illustrate how this rate of convergence can be predicted by analyzing the movement of the robots.

This paper presents the method for representing groups as Wreath Products in the context of Willefs lattice, a total ordering structure used in concept lattices for knowledge graphs. To resolve the representation issue, we utilize the Wreath Product's lattice of subgroups, an image of the group within the Willefs lattice. By leveraging the lattice of subgroups, we're able to construct the Wreath Product's representation of the group. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the Wreath Product's structure, while Section 3 outlines the derivation of the representation.

The detection capabilities of laser interferometric gravitational wave detectors are hindered by the limited sensitivity of their test mass resonators at higher frequencies. This document, primarily of interest to physicists, addresses this challenge by discussing the enhancement of the resonator sensitivity at higher frequencies through the use of optical recycling and the exploration of a novel configuration called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer (SSI). The SSI's 180-degree rotation of the typical Sagnac setup results in the cancellation of length-sensitive modes but potentially allows for the use of non-standard optical modes such as the breathing mode of the test masses. The research presented proposes the theoretical analysis of the sloshing Slinky detector's response to gravitational waves and the evaluation of the non-linear Einsteinian effects it may experience, ultimately assessing the viability of the sloshing Slinky configuration for detecting gravitational waves.

Current wireless systems face limitations in size, so future advancements in cellular technology will likely incorporate large antenna apertures and arrays. These massive setups offer improved data rates but create challenges in ensuring visibility between antennas and users, especially when non-intersecting visibility graphs are desired for applications like video conferencing. A key performance metric, non-intersecting visibility graph connectivity, measures this desire, though its computation is challenging and requires new algorithms to optimize and enhance, including stochastic access protocols. A research team's recent work investigates the application of binary backoff mechanisms in these protocols, analyzing their properties and deriving key metrics, though further information on binary backoff distribution is required to calculate certain connectivity levels.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models in performance, but comparing their scores is complicated by the model size and the lack of a consistent evaluation standard. In a study with a massive corpus of Wikipedia data containing 500 billion tokens, an 11-billion parameter Transformer model was found to underperform even a unigram model by a slight margin of 0.02 in terms of PERLEX score. A deeper analysis was carried out to understand the model's failures, which were discovered to be related to low-frequency words that the model failed to predict accurately. A simple residual learning strategy was then proposed where the $n$-gram model focuses on learning the probability of words not included in the training data. This approach was found to significantly enhance the model's performance with minimal training required. A experiment with a corpus of 50 billion tokens demonstrated that training for 200 epochs could match training for 2000 epochs in terms of language model accuracy. These findings suggest the potential for pre-training large corpora on new or low-frequency words and the need for further research into efficient text creation models.

This investigation seeks to address the challenges encountered in the field of optical character recognition when dealing with inclined text, by proposing a new inference-based method that improves accuracy. The incited innovation is based on the difficulty traditional solutions face in achieving high levels of accuracy, by suggesting a workflow that starts with the application of traditional algorithms and follows with the use of background information in the format of seven by seven bi-grids that depict the relationships between characters, by employing an automatic encoder-decoder model that has been adapted to the specific task at hand, by utilizing the inferred data to refine the bi-grid model through the application of Bayesian inference techniques in the format of a Boltzmann machine. The proposed approach is found to be effective in achieving superior results compared to the traditional solutions when evaluated on a collection of six publicly available data sets that consist of variously difficult samples of extracted information, by demonstrating the capability to accurately process complex inputs, by processing a large sample size of seven thousand images that depict various formats of printed information, by illustrating the potential to automate the process of aggregating election results, and by also proving the effectiveness of incorporating bilingual search functionality into the proposed system.

A simplified computational model is used to investigate the atmospheric circulation patterns in planetary models, taking into account the effects of rotation, thermal differences, and fluid dynamics. A three-dimensional large-eddy simulation is employed to accurately model the atmospheric behavior in a planet-like scenario, using a radiative-convective profile for the upper atmosphere and a sudden change in temperature at the boundary between the mantle and atmosphere. The resulting large-eddy simulation reveals a multi-cellular, multi-layered circulation pattern with strong vertical winds and differential heating, similar to what is observed in hot Jupiters and close Neptune-like planets. By gradually decreasing the angular velocity of the planet in a series of models, the study finds that the circulation pattern becomes more laminar and organized, with a strong equatorial jet and thermal wind balance, mirroring the conditions found in less turbulent atmospheres. On the other hand, by increasing the thermal contrast in a series of models, the study observes a more agitated circulation pattern with enhanced convection near the equator and pole regions, as well as a three-cellular circulation pattern, similar to what is observed in planets with higher thermal contrasts. The findings from the model experiments suggest that the circulation pattern and thermal distribution in the atmosphere can be used to determine the appropriate parameterizations for general circulation models, by taking into account the effects of fluid dynamics, thermal differences, and angular velocity.
This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function that is valid throughout the complex plane.

This study develops a sophisticated mathematical model described as a symmetric Gibbs state for an interacting Bose fluid using a Hamiltonian with both pairwise interactions and an external potential. The equilibrium state is characterized through its characteristic function, employing a representation in phase-space known as the random hydrodynamic quantum model. A key finding establishes the validity of this model to satisfy the local conservation laws for particle density, its flux, and momentum. Furthermore, the external potential is described as a time-dependent mean field acting upon the model. A notable contribution presents a connection between a time-dependent optimal coupling and the Levy concentration inequality. A subsequent result extends the random hydrodynamic quantum model by modifying the external field as a stochastic field affecting the particles, yielding a feasible scheme for quantum fluid dynamics simulation. A significant discovery shows that if the stochastic field represents a rate-boundary condition for pair creation from the vacuum, a rigorous relationship emerges between this rate and the Levy distance. A final contribution describes a fully dynamic scheme where the scheme and external field are integrated to simulate quantum fluid dynamics. A key finding here establishes that this dynamic mean-field scheme is related to Levy concentration rates, leading to a relationship between the field's rate of change and the Levy distance. A prominent outcome depicts the optimal interacting state as a solution to a quantum hydrodynamic equation system with a stochastic source term. A significant finding here relates the characteristic function of the interacting state to the solution of this equation system in the presence of specific initial conditions.

Over the past decade, deep learning has achieved significant success in many knowledge representation methods, including logical and non-logical approaches. While the underlying knowledge bases in these methods continue to expand, they often fail to effectively utilize the vast amount of existing information. In contrast, our focus is on constructive knowledge acquisition, where a novel, efficient approach is designed using non-logical and/or logical methods, leading to an enhanced knowledge base. This survey outlines the current state of the edge-aware knowledge customization, which has been demonstrated to be effective in various non-logical and logical tasks, and is expected to have a positive impact on multiple future applications. The article further-presents multiple technical, non-technical, and potential applications, and it is anticipated to be beneficial to both researchers and practitioners in the field of deep learning.

We provide an in-depth overview of two optimization techniques used in graphical models: maximum probability estimation and constrained optimization, with a focus on their underlying mathematical principles and algorithmic implementations. This concise summary will facilitate the application of these optimization methods in complex linguistic models and serve as a useful resource for researchers in NLP and AI communities, who may not be familiar with their technical details. We further discuss the significance of these algorithms in building graphical models and provide insights into their theoretical underpinnings. The name "maximum probability estimation" originates from its initial application in simple grammatical models, whereas the term "constrained optimization" is used to acknowledge the constraint that ensures the derived parameters remain consistent with the training data, thus reinforcing the robustness of the learned models.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. The purpose is to demonstrate that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to another algebraic structure called $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which represents the centralizer of a specific symmetric tensor within the special linear Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. A particular focus is placed on the degree two component of the central element of the Weyl algebra's $n$-th graded algebra, particularly its role in determining the centralizer. A significant finding involves the derivation of a recurrence relation for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of $Z_ {n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which is relevant to mathematical physics and quantum mechanics.

Structured test statistics is a component of structuring deep learning-based permutation tests, but its efficiency may compromise the accuracy of the tests when dealing with large-scale network structures. Paired-permutation technique enhances the structured test by utilizing random network structures, but its application is computationally intensive. Paired-permutation is particularly effective when the random network structures are small, but its benefits are limited for larger structures. To better evaluate network structures that are small to moderate in size, a new method called precise paired-permutation is proposed. It uses the paired Permons technique to further structure the learning-based random network structures, and in some cases, it can fully eliminate the need for random network structures. The precise paired-permutation is particularly effective when the random network structures are large, and it shows significant improvements over the structured and paired-permutation tests, with a 3-order of magnitude reduction in rejection rates for large-scale networks.

Our research examined the influence of initial anisotropy shape on the generation of triangular flow $v_3$ through a multiphase transport model, focusing on Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at 200 GeV. We found that triangular flow is affected by initial state fluctuations and thermal mass radiation, with an optimal occurrence density of approximately 1.5 times the critical value. Additionally, we discovered the significant contribution of directional fluctuations in initial state to the generation of triangular flow, and the model's predicted Au+Au and Cu+Cu $v_3/s$ values of approximately 2% and 3% respectively, showed good agreement with experimental data.

This study presents a new birth model composed of grid-aligned points designed for multi-target tracking systems, along with a corresponding Point Process Measure Filter (PPMF). The objective is to reduce computational demands while maintaining accurate tracking performance. The proposed method utilizes a grid-based approach to model newly entered targets, facilitating efficient calculation of the prediction density for the entire multi-target distribution. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel theoretical framework applicable to the birth model, enabling its calculation without reference to infinite grids. The proposed pmmf is an extension of the H1-BES filter, which is a well-known componentized birth-carré filter, and can be implemented using finite sets of points rather than infinite grids. Evaluation of the filter's performance includes both simulated scenarios and real-world data from an air traffic simulation, demonstrating its effectiveness in multi-target tracking.

The pandemic's impact has made non-contact methods highly valuable. To improve the efficiency of single-point laser Doppler velocimetry systems in non-contact measurements, we have developed a+distant control scheme that integrates the system with a camera for 2D scanning. The paper outlines the theoretical framework, experimental validation, and performance analysis of this integration. The results demonstrate an accurate response time of less than one millisecond and an error rate of less than one percent, making the combined system highly effective for non-contact measurements in a wide velocity range. The outcome is of significant importance to the industry.

This paper provides proofs for two key conjectures concerning the spectral and orbital stability of a system combining the Klein-Gordon equation with an anharmonic potential. By utilizing the theory of operator pairs, we demonstrate that the spectral properties of this system are equivalent to those of two decoupled linear anharmonic oscillators. Consequently, we can confirm the system's linear, spectral, and orbital stability.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying the decay products of heavy particles like $B$ mesons can be challenging due to the complex nature of the debris. During such an identification process, two main strategies are used: analyzing the decay products in relation to the laboratory frame's geometry and examining the search for specific particles that can be reconstructed. Although effective, both methods have limitations, and this paper proposes a new search for the decay of $B$ mesons into photon and axial particle candidates that are produced close to the laboratory frame's center. This type of search, which is not impacted by the losses associated with low efficiency detectors and is highly sensitive to the axial particle candidate's interaction capabilities, is found to be the most effective way of detecting these types of candidates with weak interaction abilities. In contrast, the data from existing searches for the decay products in question, which are produced with significant angles in the laboratory frame's geometry or that are difficult to reconstruct, are found to be the limiting factors in determining the axial particle candidate's interaction abilities that are produced close to the laboratory frame's center and with relatively high energy levels.

This study examines the source of errors in a system that uses contextualized language models to find words whose meanings have evolved over time. The models, including FastText, GloVe, and Word2Vec, misidentify changes in meaning based on their training data's temporal context. When the data lacks strong semantic or syntactic links to a word, the model infers meaning based on the surrounding words in each time period. To address this issue, we conducted fresh experiments on finding words with stable meanings across different time periods, such as political terms and religious concepts. The results show that these types of words can be effectively identified as their meanings tend not to change significantly over time.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), including highly variable objects like QPOs and GRBs, have sparked interest as possible sources for detecting dark matter consisting of ultralight bosons. A novel method described in this research uses the spin measurements of massive black holes to infer the mass bounds of dark matter candidates. The underlying principle involves the process of black hole superradiance, which can lead to the growth of fields around massive black holes. By analyzing the data from a sample of 24 AGNs with available spin measurements, researchers found that the current observations of electromagnetic emissions indicate the field around these black holes has not reached a state where it dominates the system's dynamics. This leads to tighter constraints on the potential dark matter consisting of ultralight bosons, especially in the range of 10^-20 to 10^-15 times the speed of light, improving upon previous mass bounds by one to three orders of magnitude in this specific frequency band.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were used to the theoretical physical community as a fundamental and engaging model that illustrates the influence of external forces on a system's driving. This driven system's unique characteristic leads to an interesting situation where the Hamiltonian changes over time, creating a challenge in solving the system's eigenvalues and eigenvectors without applicable formulas. However, this difficulty becomes particularly relevant when the driving function takes a-cosine or sine forms, eliciting a strong resonance effect under certain frequencies. Although the driving has no impact on the system's energy eigenstates, it influences the driving's observable outcomes. This paper's primary contribution forms a comprehensive and reusable path integral expression for the harmonic oscillator under the influence of external forces, enabling the calculation of various physical quantities of interest. The systematic approach allows for the computation of the driven harmonic oscillator's ground state and excited state wave functions, as well as its partition function, through numerical methods. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the determination of expectation values for quantum operators, including position, momentum, and Hamiltonian, under driven conditions. The driving's impact becomes particularly evident when calculating these expectation values, allowing researchers to observe the system's response to the force in a location and momentum space graphically. The driven quantum harmonic oscillator's physical characteristics lead to an interesting situation where the system's eigenvalues become time-independent, yet the expectation values of the driving become time-dependent under certain conditions. We have developed an expectation-based predicate for the relational Hoare logic of quantum programs to enhance its capability for establishing correctness. By leveraging the expectation framework, we are able to address pre- and post-conditions that extend beyond boolean conditions, enabling us to quantify in terms of loss or damage that may occur during a relation, as well as to specify targets for such objectives. We have derived an expectation-based relational Hoare logic for the quantum while program to facilitate the verification of such complex predicates. Our new formalism is distinct from previous work, including a quantum analog of the Garland-Hare logic and an logic developed by Kusumoto et al., and we have demonstrated its effectiveness by defining common correctness specifications for teleportation, swap, Tolerant Delete, and Tolerent Copy operations.

The paper addresses the issue of polarization angle ambiguity in weak magnetic field strengths by using a neural network to process solar magnetogram data. To evaluate the different strategies for resolving this issue, a comprehensive suite of tests was performed, including analysis of magnetic field structure, gradient, and spin properties, as well as comparison with observed Stokes V data. The results revealed that an optimal solution would take into account the polarization angle, magnetic field intensity, and the data's spin characteristics, leading to a more accurate and physically meaningful map of the solar surface's magnetic field structure.

The grid diagram of a non-degenerate complex manifold is described by the polynomial ring associated with the complex manifold in question. Specifically, for the manifold $r$ dimensions deep, let's denote the resulting boolean ring as $M_{n_{r}}$; consequently, the grid diagram of the product of orthogonal reflections $i!$ over itself is represented by the product's grid diagram. By examining the grid diagrams of various manifold configurations, we can derive the grid diagram corresponding to a specific manifold in question. This method is then applied to the double manifold of a rational curve, revealing its polynomial ring structure. Moreover, the grid diagram of the product of two involutions over a complex manifold is demonstrated to have a cubic lattice structure, thereby establishing the cubic lattice as well as the diagonal lattice within its reach. Additionally, by investigating the manifold's stable equivalence, we can obtain a more extensive grid diagram, revealing its four-by-four lattice in question; this is a further extension of the results obtained thus far.

A space curve is classified as a Bertrand curve when there's a relation between its curvature and torsion, known as its involute. In 1885, Bonnet described such curves as having a special geometric property. Then in 1899, Bonnet further defined a curve as a Bertrand curve when a specific geometric condition is met. The term "Bertrand curve" was likely coined by Godey in 1900, although he used slightly different terminology. While the original discussions focused on Euclidean 3-space, French mathematicians had previously considered the problem in the context of the Minkowski plane. The aim of this paper is to provide a comprehensive overview of the geometric features of Timelike Bertrand curves in Minkowski 3-space, including a detailed analysis of their polynomial version, and also explore the relevance of these curves in various applications.

The robustness of deep learning systems has been compromised by adversarial examples, prompting a shift from theoretical to practical analysis. Particularly, the relevance of adversarial attacks might not be significantly impacted by the loss function used, leading to a discussion on its importance. The potential benefit of using modified loss functions, which may enhance a classifier's resistance to attacks, is also explored. The effectiveness of this improvement is promising but not definitively proven. The possible cause for the modified loss function's beneficial effect is the closer proximity of the gradient to the true gradient, suggesting a possible explanation. The hypothesis that this benefit stems from the closer proximity of the gradient to the true gradient is not confirmed. Various modification strategies are examined through experiments, with the outcome revealing that modified loss functions do not necessarily result in greater test accuracy compared to the true cross-entropy loss function. The reason for this outcome is not clearly explained. The possible cause for the modified loss function's beneficial effect is the closer proximity of the gradient to the true gradient, suggesting a possible explanation. The benefit of the modified loss function in terms of test accuracy is not guaranteed, as demonstrated by experimental outcomes. The reason for this outcome is not clearly explained.

This study establishes that machines can acquire the ability to infer cause-and-effect relationships between events specific to real-world situations. To support this ability, we've assembled a comprehensive collection of 386 causal principles universal to machines, each with the following information provided: a descriptive name, detailed explanation, five relevant examples with descriptions and outcomes, and a structured summary consisting of two parts - a general rule and specific instances. Furthermore, we've carried out the application of these principles in a series of testing scenarios to demonstrate their effectiveness in enabling machines to deduce new information from observed events. Our testing procedure involves a multiple-choice assessment consisting of 133 testing instances, as well as an eleven-turn dialogue task designed to mimic the accumulation of information in an interactive setting. Our findings indicate that the integration of these principles into modeling significantly enhances the ability to infer new information from observed events, compared to standard approaches. In addition to this finding, we've created an online resource cataloging all of the following: the atlas of machine-common knowledge, a demonstration environment, and a multiple-choice reasoning task, which can be accessed at the following URL: https://atomic-atlas.ai/.

To predict future frames in dynamic video scenes, particularly in retail environments like convenient stores, a method called Innovative View Video Forecasting (INV2) is described. This environment involves monitoring activities around a shelf's stock levels. The challenge lies in generating high-resolution videos from limited information available. To address this, a dual representation system is employed, combining auto-encoder and VQ-VAE models to create a more effective feature expression. Following this, an attention-based generative model is used to predict future frames. The effectiveness of this system has been confirmed through experiments, showing significant improvements over existing methods, particularly in generating camera views not seen during training.

This study examines the intersection of theoretical computer science and robotics, specifically the concept of robot navigation within a graph structure. A rectangular robot is depicted with the capability to traverse the graph's vertices and edges, identifying edges as point-like and vertices as short segments. The rectangular robot's task is to distinguish between all the vertices in the graph by observing the distances it perceives to an unknown but fixed set of reference nodes (special vertices). The goal is to determine the minimum size of this set of reference nodes. This problem is identified as the "metric dimension" problem, which is then re-explored with the objective of finding the minimal size of this set while excluding the most redundant vertex from the calculation, resulting in the shorted metric dimension. This new variable is applied to various graph structures including complete graphs, cyclic graphs, and various tree-like structures as well as their combinations.

This research focuses on categorizing heart sounds into two main categories: normal heart sounds (M1) and pathological heart sounds (M2), with a specific emphasis on a certain type of pathology known as murmur.  The  goal is to improve the classification of these sounds, which can provide crucial diagnostic information for healthcare professionals.  To achieve this improvement, the study proposes two main strategies: an iterative method that combines additive noise and convolutional deformation, as well as a sequential method that alternates between the same factors.  To evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches, the paper uses a dataset consisting of 1600 WAV files, with the files pre-processed by normalizing their energy levels and resampling them to a uniform rate of 11020 Hz.  The proposed methods were tested and shown to outperform the baseline M1 network in terms of accuracy in heart sound categorization.

We examine the production of the low excitation intervals of the neutral atomic carbon spectrum ($\lambda\lambda$ 909, 833 nm) within galaxies, focusing on their observed enhancement in a molecular gas-rich environment. A theoretical prediction had anticipated these specific spectral lines would be suppressed in such environments due to the cold temperatures and low densities prevailing within them. However, observations have demonstrated that the stellar mass growth rate of galaxies experiences an acceleration when the intensity of the $\lambda\833\,{\rm nm}$ line increases, despite unexpected findings that defy conventional thermal physics principles. A non-thermal mechanism is proposed to explain this anomaly, involving the non-Maxwellian distribution of gas particle speeds and the population inversion of the atomic carbon's energy states. A suitable name for the phenomenon, nonthermal atomic carbon inversion radiative cooling (NAIC cooling), has been suggested to describe this process, its observability through spectroscopy in the near-infrared spectrum, and its relevance to understanding molecular gas reservoirs within galaxies has been discussed in detail. In addition, the potential of utilizing the intensity of the $\lambda\833\,{\rm nm}$ line as a momentum transfer rate meter, and even as a supplement to the $CO$-based temperature and density estimation methods, in future hydrodynamical simulations of star formation within galaxies, has been explored in greater depth.

We identify the velocity changes experienced by specific particle configurations in ASEP, including symmetric ASEP, ASEP with linear external fields, and ASEP with linear external fields when parity is preserved, within the ASEP model with external fields when considering its dynamics on a one-dimensional lattice when we're interested in its asymptotic behavior as time tends to infinity.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has spurred a surge in research on mathematical models outlining the spread of infectious diseases. As the epidemic enters a new phase with widespread vaccination and changes in human behavior, there is an urgent need for models that can effectively support decision-making processes. Although numerous reviews have been published detailing various mathematical models and their uses, they often fall short in connecting model components to specific aspects of the disease and its dynamics. This paper aims to address this gap by providing a comprehensive guide on mathematical models relevant to the COVID-19 pandemic, its control measures, and associated data. It outlines the fundamental characteristics of the virus, its symptoms, data types, and the basic model components including basic reproduction number, generation interval, and serial interval. It also describes more advanced model features such as the R0 value, generation time distribution, and the use of compartmental, individual-based, and network models for describing the spread of the virus, as well as the dynamics of immune responses and the potential for treatment and vaccination. The paper concludes by suggesting areas for future research. This review will be particularly useful for public health professionals, policymakers, and journalists, enabling them to better interpret study findings on the COVID-19 pandemic.

Bulges within galaxies are believed to be key in determining the decrease in star formation seen in massive galaxies compared to star-forming bulgeless galaxies of their size. To examine the impact of bulges on the star formation main sequence breaking point at the most massive end, we investigated a sample of 1464 galaxies weighing between 10^10.5 and 10^11.0 solar masses within the z=0.2 range, utilizing optical spectral data from the MAST database. We classified these galaxies into three groups: those with bulge-dominant structures, those without significant bulges, and those with intermediate features, employing a B/T ratio threshold of 0.3 to distinguish between bulgeless and bulge dominant galaxies. When dividing these galaxies into low mass categories of -25,-21, and -19 ergs s^-1 cm^-2, corresponding to B/T ratios of 0, 0.5, and 1.0, we found that bulgeless galaxies tend to have lower star formation rates relative to the sequence and specific star formation rates in all three categories in comparison to bulge-dominant galaxies of the same B/T0 value. This study investigates the application of multi-task learning to the analysis of
sentiments in Italian and English simultaneously. The system incorporates a pre-trained
model (BERT) alongside two distinct techniques: indirect transfer learning and a combined
approach that integrates indirect transfer learning with multi-task learning. Evaluations
were conducted on three datasets: English (Stanford), which consists of movie reviews,
and two Italian datasets (IAST and IATST) comprising tweets. Indirect transfer learning
demonstrated improved outcomes compared to direct methods, while the proposed multi-task
learning strategy further enhanced the analysis of sentiments in the iatst dataset.

This study examines the findings of a paper by Wang et al.(2019) confirming the presence of a planetary body within a star's surface of WD1145+017, an anomalous white dwarf, based on its transiting behavior. However, as the observed transiting profile does not cause the white dwarf to accrete significant amounts of hydrogen, the authors' conclusion that the transiting debris is responsible for the WD1145+017 losing its atmospheric layers may be flawed. Instead, theWD1145+017's atmospheric depletion could have been caused by angular momentum loss through radiative processes, and the transiting debris observed is likely unconnected to these losses, potentially consisting of a nearby body that will eventually enter the white dwarf's influence sphere.

The rapid proliferation of social media has given rise to fraudulent activities, particularly the creation and dissemination of false multimedia content, which can be costly and damaging. While existing methods for detecting false news have achieved some success, their effectiveness may be limited when dealing with the diversity of content that pervades media-rich environments. In an effort to tackle this challenge, our proposed framework, METEONET, is designed to enable the system to adapt to the detection of false content without the need for extensive labeled data, which is often difficult and expensive to obtain. By leveraging the power of meta-learning and neural process networks, our system can achieve accurate detection of false content by learning from a small number of examples, i.e., reliable ground truth data. As demonstrated through extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, including Twitter, our proposed framework outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, showing an improvement of 4.7%, 10.2% and 2.1% in F1 score in comparison to the best existing model. Further analysis reveals the effectiveness of the proposed components and the practical potential of the system for detecting the spread of false content on social media platforms.

This research has developed three types of novel Golay complementary sequence pairs PRC, IRC, and GRC to expand the known lower bounds for sizes of SGCS and GGC sets families. Firstly, an method combines two family sets of PRC/IRC/GRC to generate a new family of SGCS/GGC. Secondly, three family sets of PRC, IRC, and GGC are orthogonal within themselves, allowing the formation of larger families of Golay complementary sets. Consequently, enhanced bounds for the sizes of SGCS and GGC families are derived. Specifically, new family size lower bounds are achieved for both sparse PRC/IRC and GRC sets. Notably, the largest family sizes of SGCS and GGC are possible when set lengths are 850, 950, and 1000, surpassing previous records for medium to large family sizes.

Medical imaging techniques such as MRI and CT scans provide detailed anatomical information but lack functional insights. To enhance the insight into a'seamless' medical imaging technique, researchers have developed methods to produce defects in images that correspond to specific areas of the brain responsible for various functions and knowledge-based patterns that describe those regions. However, existing image defect generation models are not suitable for creating customized defects that meet the necessary standards. Our proposed approach, a progressive training framework based on the Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (AIVE), aims to produce high-fidelity and informative lesions in medical images. Experimental results from multiple datasets, including MS-COVO and FS-COVO, demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in producing defect-free images and the effectiveness of the AIVE network in producing high-quality lesions. The results indicate that the proposed technique yields superior outcomes compared to other existing models.

We present a novel approach to managing multiple types of relational data, addressing both binary and non-binary relationships. Our method, which is primarily a neural network-based framework, is designed to infer the characteristics of an entity within the data set. Our notable achievement in managing relational data, which serves as a comprehensive framework, has successfully managed three distinct data types: binary relational data, which is a type of data that represents the relationship between two entities; a variation that relates an entity with another; and a approach that determines the target entity with the highest correlation to a given entity. Our framework, which is primarily a neural network-based model, is designed to infer the characteristics of an entity within the data set. Our method has demonstrated superior performance when tested on three different sets of data, which represent three different types of relationships between entities, outperforming existing approaches in literature.

Recent advances in capabilities and efficiency drive the rapid growth of LLM-based models. While the GPT-4 based model demonstrates high performance on a wide variety of tasks, its and the training of the model are both highly resource-intensive. This becomes a major obstacle when a new task requires the model's retraining or the development of a specialized framework. To address this, we propose a new approach that enables a large pre-trained model to effectively perform a wide range of knowledge-based tasks with high accuracy. This capability allows the Large pre-trained model to access and utilize structured external knowledge without the need for the model's retraining or the use of a complex framework, thus saving costs. We call this new capacity "structured knowledge integration" and demonstrate through extensive experiments on multiple datasets that our method, Ability, achieves consistent results that surpass both the GPT-4 based model and other similar frameworks. This proves the potential of our structured external knowledge approach. To further illustrate the effectiveness of Ability, we create a new dataset, SICK, that the large pre-trained model can efficiently use to expand its capabilities without the need for the model's retraining. This shows the practical benefits of our structured external knowledge approach.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in the QED paradigm. We examine the impact this interaction has on black hole thermodynamics when a charge is applied to the system and a nonlinear radiation field is generated. Through an equivalent circuit model, we analyze the effects of nonlinearity on a charged AdS black hole in the context of shadow thermodynamics. We find that as the radiation field intensifies and the black hole's horizon radius decreases, the image of the black hole's horizon enlarges when a nonlinearity occurs. We also observe that the nonlinear interaction amplifies the occurrence of thermal nonequilibrium between the black hole and the radiation field. Moreover, we discover that the nonlinearity results in the emergence of an additional phase point where the black hole's thermal nonequilibrium can be balanced. We further analyze the relationship between the charge and the nonlinear interaction and observe that the interaction has a more significant impact on the black hole's nonequilibrium when there is a higher initial charge. We also investigate the effect of nonlinearity on the thermal nonequilibrium phase and find that it causes the phase to shrink. We discuss these findings in detail.

Synchronized onset and improvements in entanglement are critical areas in quantum information theory. The complex dynamics of interaction between continuous variable operators and the quantum entanglement between subsystems in a two-partite system have drawn our interest. By examining the modifications in entanglement in response to the operator interaction, we are able to visualize both the synchronized onset and enhancement patterns in entanglement through the tomographic image. The complex correlations between operator alterations and changes in entanglement have been found to exhibit straightforward connections through our research. The significant role that specific patterns of alterations in continuous variable operators play in the overall dynamics of the system have been highlighted. The research findings are crucial for comprehending the complexities of quantum information theory.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ branching fraction is estimated at (3.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) x10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.7±0.6±0.3±0.3±0.6) x10^-4, where the uncertainties are due to sample size, branching fraction estimates, isospin effects, $d/s$ quark mixing, and normalization respectively.

In a graded module over a Coxeter group, particularly a Hecke algebra, the lattice of submodules forms a Frobenius extension. Since lattice theory and K-theory are closely linked, it is possible to construct the lattice of submodules from the K-group ring, which is possible when the module's graded components correspond to ideals in the ring. This construction is especially relevant in the study of representations of Coxeter groups, where the module in question, $V$, has submodules corresponding to the subrepresentations. Notably, in the case of the permutation representation of a Coxeter group, subrepresentations map to ideal structures, enabling the construction of the lattice of submodules from the (ideal) ideal lattice. This is particularly useful as it allows us to determine the subrepresentations of certain modules, such as the module associated with non-changeable edges in a diagram, of graphs with a given symmetry group. The resulting lattice of ideals is an interest semilattice, providing valuable information about the modules' representations.

We explore how a linear combination of a biharmonic hypersurface being isotropic in Euclidean space equates to its mean curvature being harmonic. We also discuss its relationship with constant scalar curvature and its potential for being constant. Additionally, we investigate the connection with harmonic functions on the shape operator and their relation to hypersurfaces with a single isometry-invariant tensor, as well as their equivalence with having a shape operator that satisfies a certain differential equation. We then define biharmonic hypersurfaces that satisfy this condition as repetitive biharmonic hypersurfaces. We then summarize the characterization of repetitive biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, which consist of a few specific cases involving products of Euclidean spaces and spheres, as well as products of hyperbolic and spherical spaces, and their corresponding operators that satisfy the relevant equation. We also discuss how this result is a extension of a previous result.

A integer fraction p/q represents a rational number that corresponds to a infinite sequence of digits in base q after the decimal point. A finite sequence of base q digits can be turned into an infinite sequence by repeating it an infinite number of times to form a p/q-sequence. Some subsets of all possible p/q-sequences are known as p/q-identifiable sets, where the characteristic function of each such set can be represented as a infinite polynomial in base q. This research is relevant to the theory of automatic sequences and its applications in coding theory and data security. A significant result is the translation of previous theorems into more general forms, including the determination of the entropy of the optimal encoder for identifiable sets and its connection to the maximum block that can be changed to correct an error.
